name: Egusi soup

difficulty.label: Intermediate
drivers: Egusi scorches fast if the heat is too high — it needs watching
Two things run at once: the meat boils while you build the egusi
Getting the 'fried, not raw' egusi texture takes a little judgement

time.overlap_note: Do the grinding and chopping while the meat boils — real time on your feet is closer to 45-50 min.
make_ahead: Boil the beef the night before and refrigerate

equipment: Blender or dry mill (unless egusi is pre-ground)

ingredients.prep: Ground to a coarse powder. Buy it pre-ground, or blend the dry seeds in a dry mill until it looks like damp sand. You do NOT pour whole seeds into the pot.
Cut into pieces. Beef needs ~40 min to get tender; kpomo ~20 min.
Wash and tear by hand into small pieces. If bitter leaf, squeeze it in 2-3 changes of water first.

steps.action: Season the meat with half the onion, a stock cube and salt, then boil with just enough water to cover it until tender. Keep the meat stock — don't throw it away.
steps.cue: A fork slides into the beef with no resistance.
steps.why: Tough Nigerian beef will never soften inside the soup later — it has to be cooked through first. This is the step the old recipe skipped, which is why its timing was wrong.
steps.watch_out: Start this first and do all the prep below while it boils.

steps.action: Grind the egusi to a coarse powder if it isn't already ground.
steps.cue: Texture of coarse, slightly damp sand — not a smooth paste.
steps.why: Whole melon seeds can't thicken the soup. Milling them is what makes egusi 'egusi'.
steps.watch_out: Don't over-blend or the oil comes out and it turns to paste. Pulse it.

steps.action: Heat the palm oil in a clean pot on medium for 1 minute, add the sliced onion and stir until see-through (translucent, soft, not browned).
steps.cue: Onion goes glassy and soft, about 3 minutes.
steps.why: Softening the onion first builds the base flavour.
steps.watch_out: Palm oil should shimmer, not smoke. If it smokes, it's too hot — take it off the heat for 30 seconds.

steps.action: Add the ground egusi to the oil and stir constantly. It will clump — that's correct. Keep stirring as it toasts.
steps.cue: It smells nutty and the colour deepens slightly, about 3-4 minutes.
steps.why: Toasting the egusi in oil is what gives the soup its signature flavour and stops it tasting raw and floury.
steps.watch_out: This is the scorch point. The moment it smells burnt instead of nutty, drop the heat — burnt egusi can't be saved.

steps.action: Pour in the reserved meat stock a little at a time, stirring the egusi clumps into it. Add the cooked meat. Cover and simmer on low.
steps.cue: The egusi softens and small balls of it float in a thickened broth.
steps.why: Adding the hot stock gradually keeps the egusi in soft lumps instead of one dense mass.
steps.watch_out: Too thick? Add more stock or water. Too thin? Simmer uncovered a few minutes.

steps.action: Stir in the ground crayfish and taste for salt.
steps.cue: It tastes savoury and slightly smoky.
steps.why: Crayfish is the umami backbone. Season at the end so you don't over-salt.

steps.action: Add the torn ugu or bitter leaf, stir once, cover for 2 minutes, then turn off the heat.
steps.cue: The greens wilt but stay green.
steps.why: Greens cook in residual heat. Boiling them dulls the colour and flavour.
steps.watch_out: Don't cook the leaves long — they only need to wilt.

doneness_signature: Thick, nutty soup with soft egusi lumps, a film of red palm oil on top, and bright-green wilted leaves.

rescue.fix: There's no recovery — burnt egusi flavours the whole pot. Start the egusi step again with fresh ground egusi and add it to the existing broth.
Skim the excess palm oil off the top with a spoon, or simmer uncovered to cook some of it down.
Add more crayfish and a little salt, not just stock cube. The savoury depth comes from crayfish.

level_up.how: Add a small piece of stockfish or smoked fish to the meat while it boils.
Stir in a teaspoon of ground ogiri or iru (locust bean) with the crayfish.

name: Jollof rice

difficulty.label: Simple
drivers: One main technique: frying the tomato base until the rawness goes
Forgiving — the main risk is rice cooking unevenly, fixed by low heat

time.overlap_note: The protein boils while you blend and fry the base.

equipment: Heavy pot with a tight lid

ingredients.prep: Washed in cold water until the water runs clear.

steps.action: Season the protein with some onion, a stock cube and salt, then cook in a pot with a little water until done. Set the meat aside and KEEP the stock water.
steps.cue: Chicken ~15 min, beef ~30-40 min, until tender.
steps.why: The stock water carries flavour straight into the rice. This is the secret to jollof that isn't bland.
steps.watch_out: Don't let it boil dry — keep a cup of stock at the end.

steps.action: In a dry pot, heat the oil for 1 minute, add half the sliced onion and fry until golden.
steps.cue: Onions turn golden, about 3 minutes.
steps.why: Golden onions sweeten and deepen the base.
steps.watch_out: Don't blacken them — golden, not burnt.

steps.action: Pour in the blended tomato-pepper mix. Let it FRY (not boil) on medium, stirring every 2 minutes, until the raw tomato smell is gone and it darkens.
steps.cue: The mix thickens, darkens to a deep red, and oil starts to show at the edges.
steps.why: Frying out the raw tomato is the single thing that separates real jollof from tomato-rice. Don't shortcut it.
steps.watch_out: It will splatter. Pour slowly and lower the heat if it spits.

steps.action: Add the reserved stock water, curry, and taste for salt. Then add the washed rice and stir so every grain is coated. Liquid should sit just above the rice.
steps.cue: Liquid level is roughly 1cm above the rice.
steps.why: Too much liquid = mushy; too little = crunchy. Just above the rice is right.
steps.watch_out: Add water, not more stock, if you misjudge — the base is already seasoned.

steps.action: Cover with foil then the lid, and cook on the LOWEST heat. Check at 25 minutes.
steps.cue: Rice is soft with no chalky crunch in the centre of a grain.
steps.why: Foil traps steam so the top layer cooks; lowest heat lets it steam without burning the bottom.
steps.watch_out: Resist stirring early — it breaks the grains. A little crust at the bottom (the 'party jollof' bottom) is a feature, not a fault.

doneness_signature: Each grain separate, deep orange-red, smoky, with the rice tender all the way through.

rescue.problem: Rice is crunchy but liquid is gone
rescue.fix: Sprinkle 1/4 cup hot water over the top, cover, and steam on the lowest heat 8-10 more minutes.
Take the lid off and cook on low to dry it out, fluffing gently with a fork.
Don't stir the burnt part up. Move the pot to the lowest heat or off the flame, lid on, and let the steam finish it.

level_up.how: In the last 10 minutes, let the bottom catch very slightly on low heat for that charred 'bottom pot' flavour.
Add a blended red bell pepper (tatashe) to the base — brighter red, milder, sweeter.

name: Fried rice

difficulty.label: Intermediate
drivers: Timing: the rice must be cooked ahead and cooled, or it turns to mush
High-heat stir-frying needs you to keep things moving
Several components prepped and added in the right order

time.overlap_note: Boil and cool the rice ahead of time; the stir-fry itself is fast.
make_ahead: Boil the rice and spread it to cool (even the night before)

equipment: Wide plate or tray for cooling rice

ingredients.prep: Boiled in salted water until JUST cooked, drained, and spread out to cool completely.
Seasoned and fried or grilled separately, then diced.

steps.action: Boil the rice in salted water until just cooked — still firm, not soft. Drain and spread it on a wide plate to cool completely.
steps.cue: Grains are cooked through but still firm; fully cool to the touch before frying.
steps.why: Warm, wet rice steams and clumps in the pan. Cool, dry rice fries into separate grains. This is the whole secret to fried rice.
steps.watch_out: Under-boil slightly rather than over — it cooks more in the pan.

steps.action: Heat the oil in a wide pan or wok on HIGH heat, add the onion and stir for 1 minute.
steps.cue: Onion sizzles loudly the moment it hits the pan.
steps.why: High heat is what gives stir-fry its flavour. A cool pan steams the vegetables.
steps.watch_out: Keep everything moving on high heat so nothing scorches.

steps.action: Add the carrots and green beans. Stir-fry on high for 3-4 minutes.
steps.cue: Vegetables are bright and still have a slight crunch.
steps.why: Quick high-heat cooking keeps colour and bite.
steps.watch_out: Don't cook them soft and grey — they should stay vivid.

steps.action: Add the cooled rice. Stir-fry, lifting and tossing, for 2-3 minutes so every grain gets oil.
steps.cue: Grains separate and glisten.
steps.why: Tossing coats the grains and reheats them without making them wet.
steps.watch_out: If it clumps, your rice was too warm — break clumps gently with the back of the spoon.

steps.action: Add soy sauce, taste, and adjust with stock cube and salt. Stir in the cooked protein and heat through for 1 minute.
steps.cue: Even colour, savoury taste, protein hot.
steps.why: Adding protein last keeps it from drying out.
steps.watch_out: Soy sauce is salty — taste before adding more salt.

doneness_signature: Separate, glossy grains flecked with bright vegetables, evenly coloured, savoury and hot.

rescue.fix: Spread it out on a tray off the heat to release steam, then return to the hot pan in batches.
A little more soy sauce and stock cube. Colour comes from soy, not water.

level_up.how: Add a clove of minced garlic and a thumb of grated ginger with the onion.
Push the rice aside, scramble an egg in the empty space, then fold it through.

name: Efo riro (Nigerian vegetable soup)

difficulty.label: Simple
drivers: One judgement call: frying the pepper base until the oil floats
Forgiving — the main rule is don't overcook the greens

time.overlap_note: Pre-cook tough proteins like kpomo or stockfish while you blend and shred.

ingredients.prep: Blended together (leave it slightly chunky for texture).

steps.action: If using kpomo or stockfish, pre-cook it in salted water until soft. Set aside.
steps.cue: Kpomo is soft and chewy, not rubbery.
steps.why: These never soften in the soup itself.
steps.watch_out: Skip this step if your protein is already tender.

steps.action: Heat the palm oil in a pot, add the onion and fry 2 minutes until soft.
steps.cue: Onion soft and fragrant.
steps.why: Base flavour.
steps.watch_out: Don't smoke the palm oil.

steps.action: Pour in the blended tomato-pepper. Fry on medium, stirring, until the oil floats to the top.
steps.cue: A clear film of red oil rises to the surface — the sign the rawness is cooked out.
steps.why: The floating-oil cue is how every Nigerian cook knows the base is done. Trust it over the clock.
steps.watch_out: It spits as it thickens — keep the heat at medium and stir.

steps.action: Add the protein, crayfish and stock cube. Taste for salt and stir.
steps.cue: Savoury, well-seasoned base.
steps.why: Season before the greens so you don't overwork them.

steps.action: Add the shredded greens, stir once, and cover for about 3 minutes. Then take off the heat.
steps.cue: Greens wilt but stay vivid green.
steps.why: The green colour is the sign you cooked it right. Overcooking turns it khaki and flat.
steps.watch_out: Spinach wilts faster than ugu — check at 2 minutes for spinach.

doneness_signature: Glossy red, oil-rich base studded with bright-green wilted leaves and tender protein.

rescue.fix: Can't reverse it, but stir in a small handful of fresh shredded greens off the heat for colour.
Simmer uncovered a few minutes before adding the greens.

level_up.how: Add a teaspoon of locust bean (iru) with the crayfish for a savoury, fermented note.
Throw in a few cubes of pre-fried liver or ponmo at the end.

name: Ofe onugbu (bitter leaf soup)

difficulty.label: Involved
drivers: Bitter leaf must be washed and squeezed many times or the soup is inedibly bitter
Cocoyam has to be boiled and pounded into a thickener — a whole sub-task
Several components and a long total time to coordinate

time.overlap_note: Boil the cocoyam and meat while you wash and squeeze the bitter leaf.
make_ahead: Wash and squeeze the bitter leaf

equipment: Mortar and pestle (or a blender for the cocoyam)

ingredients.prep: Washed and squeezed hard in 4-5 changes of water until only mildly bitter.
Boiled until soft (~30 min), peeled, and pounded to a smooth paste.
substitutes: cocoyam flour (achi or ofor as alternative thickener)

steps.action: Wash the bitter leaf in 4-5 changes of water, squeezing hard each time. Taste a piece — it should be only slightly bitter, not harsh.
steps.cue: A leaf tastes mildly bitter, pleasant rather than punishing.
steps.why: This is the make-or-break step. Under-washed bitter leaf ruins the whole pot. The old recipe hid this 12-minute task in the ingredient list.
steps.watch_out: Pre-washed packaged bitter leaf skips most of this — just rinse it.

steps.action: Boil the cocoyam corms until soft, peel them, and pound to a smooth, stretchy paste.
steps.cue: Paste is smooth and elastic with no lumps.
steps.why: Pounded cocoyam is the traditional thickener — it gives the soup its body and pull.
steps.watch_out: Lumps won't dissolve later, so pound thoroughly. A blender with a splash of water works too.

steps.action: Boil the meat and stockfish with onion, stock cube and salt until tender. Keep the stock.
steps.cue: Meat is tender; stockfish is soft.
steps.why: Builds the savoury base liquid.
steps.watch_out: Overlaps with the steps above — run them together.

steps.action: Add the palm oil to the stock and bring to a boil. Drop the pounded cocoyam in small lumps and stir to dissolve.
steps.cue: The lumps melt in and the soup thickens and turns glossy.
steps.why: Boiling stock dissolves the cocoyam evenly into a thick body.
steps.watch_out: Add cocoyam gradually — you can always add more to thicken, but you can't un-thicken easily.

steps.action: Stir in the crayfish and ogiri, simmer 8-10 minutes.
steps.cue: Rich, earthy aroma; soup coats the spoon.
steps.why: Ogiri gives onugbu its deep traditional flavour.

steps.action: Add the bitter leaf, cook 5 minutes, and taste.
steps.cue: Rich, earthy, and only pleasantly bitter.
steps.why: The bitter leaf goes in near the end so it stays tender.
steps.watch_out: Still too bitter? You under-washed in step 1 — there's no fix now except to dilute with more stock.

doneness_signature: Thick, dark, glossy soup with a deep earthy aroma and a clean, mild bitterness.

rescue.fix: Dilute with extra stock or water and re-season. Next time wash the leaf in more changes of water.
Pound and add a little more cocoyam, or a teaspoon of cocoyam flour slaked in water.
Mash the lumps against the side of the pot and simmer until they melt in.

level_up.how: Add a mix of assorted meats — shaki, ponmo, and dry fish — for a celebration-grade pot.

name: Beans and fried plantain

difficulty.label: Simple
drivers: Mostly hands-off, but the beans take a long time to soften
Frying plantain needs the right ripeness and a watchful eye

time.overlap_note: Fry the plantain while the beans simmer.
make_ahead: Soak the beans 30+ min to cut cooking time

ingredients.prep: Washed; soak 30 min if you have time — it speeds cooking.
Yellow-with-black-spots for sweetness. Peeled and sliced.

steps.action: Boil the beans with the onion in plenty of water until soft.
steps.cue: A bean squashes easily between two fingers.
steps.why: Beans must be fully soft before seasoning — salt added too early keeps them hard.
steps.watch_out: Top up with hot water if it dries out. Soaked beans cook faster.

steps.action: When soft, drain off most of the water leaving about 1 cup. Add palm oil, crayfish, stock cube and salt. Simmer 10 minutes.
steps.cue: Thick, porridge-like, glossy with palm oil.
steps.why: Now that the beans are soft, the seasoning soaks in.
steps.watch_out: Stir so it doesn't catch on the bottom.

steps.action: While the beans simmer, peel and slice the plantains on the diagonal.
steps.cue: Even slices fry evenly.
steps.why: Diagonal slices give more golden surface.

steps.action: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a pan and fry the plantain slices until golden-brown on each side. Salt lightly.
steps.cue: Deep golden, caramelised edges, soft inside.
steps.why: Ripe plantain caramelises — that sweetness is the point.
steps.watch_out: Medium heat — too hot burns the outside before the inside softens.

steps.action: Serve the beans with the fried plantain alongside.
steps.why: The sweet plantain balances the earthy beans.

doneness_signature: Soft, glossy, palm-oil-rich beans next to sweet, deep-golden fried plantain.

rescue.problem: Beans still hard after a long time
rescue.fix: Keep simmering with hot water; never add salt or cold water while they're hardening. A pinch of baking soda speeds it up.
Lower the heat and give it more time per side.

level_up.how: Mash some of the beans and add a blended pepper-tomato mix to turn it into a richer beans porridge.

name: Nigerian pepper soup

difficulty.label: Simple
drivers: Mostly hands-off simmering
The one skill is balancing the heat level to taste

time.overlap_note: Crush the pepper and tear the leaves while the protein simmers.

ingredients.prep: Cleaned and cut. Catfish: scald with hot water and rub off the slime first.

substitutes: ground calabash nutmeg + uda + uziza seed mix

steps.action: Put the protein in a pot with enough water to cover, add the onion, stock cube, salt and pepper-soup spice, and bring to a boil.
steps.cue: A rolling boil with the spice aroma rising.
steps.why: Building the broth and cooking the protein at once.
steps.watch_out: Catfish needs less time and breaks easily — handle gently.

steps.action: Crush or blend the peppers chunky (not smooth) while it cooks.
steps.cue: Chunky pepper pieces, not a paste.
steps.why: Chunky pepper gives pepper soup its rustic texture and heat pockets.

steps.action: Add the crushed pepper after the protein has cooked ~15 minutes. Taste for heat and salt.
steps.cue: Broth is fragrant, spicy to your liking, protein is tender.
steps.why: Adding pepper partway lets you control the final heat.
steps.watch_out: Too hot to fix later — add pepper gradually.

steps.action: Add crayfish (if using) and the torn scent leaf or uziza in the last 2 minutes. Don't boil the leaves.
steps.cue: Leaves wilt and release their aroma.
steps.why: The fresh-herb aroma is the soul of pepper soup; boiling kills it.
steps.watch_out: Turn off the heat right after the leaves go in.

doneness_signature: Clear, spicy, aromatic broth with tender protein and the unmistakable scent-leaf perfume.

rescue.fix: Add more water and a touch more stock cube and salt to rebalance.
Add a little more pepper-soup spice and a fresh handful of torn scent leaf at the end.

level_up.how: Use fresh catfish steaks and add a few yam cubes to simmer in the broth for a fuller bowl.

name: Okra soup

difficulty.label: Simple
drivers: Fast, but timing-sensitive: overcooked okra loses its 'draw'
One technique — slicing the okra thin for more stretch

time.overlap_note: Slice the okra while the protein pre-cooks.

ingredients.prep: Washed and sliced thin — the thinner, the more 'draw'.

steps.action: Pre-cook the protein in salted water with onion until done. Keep the stock.
steps.cue: Protein tender.
steps.why: Tough proteins won't soften in the short okra cook.
steps.watch_out: Skip if your protein is already tender.

steps.action: Add the palm oil to the protein pot and bring to a gentle boil.
steps.cue: Oil melts into the stock.
steps.why: Base for the soup.

steps.action: Stir in the crayfish and stock cube. Taste.
steps.cue: Savoury broth.
steps.why: Season before the okra so you don't overstir it later.

steps.action: Add the sliced okra. Cook on medium for EXACTLY 5 minutes — no longer.
steps.cue: Lift the spoon: the soup stretches and 'draws' in strings.
steps.why: The draw is the whole point. Overcooking breaks it down and the soup goes watery and dull.
steps.watch_out: Set a timer. Five minutes, then stop.

steps.action: Serve immediately.
steps.cue: Hot, glossy, stretchy.
steps.why: Okra soup waits for no one — the draw fades as it sits.

doneness_signature: Glossy green soup that stretches into strings off the spoon, studded with protein.

rescue.fix: Stir in a small handful of fresh grated okra and cook just 2 more minutes.
Loosen with a splash of hot stock.

level_up.how: Add prawns and periwinkle in the last 3 minutes for a coastal-style pot.

name: Nigerian red stew (all-purpose)

difficulty.label: Simple
drivers: One real technique: frying the tomato base long enough
Splatter management when the hot oil meets the blend

time.overlap_note: Fry the protein while the blend reduces.

substitutes: tinned tomato + fresh pepper + tomato paste

ingredients.prep: Half blended into the mix, half sliced.

steps.action: Season the protein, then fry or bake it until golden-brown outside. Set aside. Keep any juices.
steps.cue: Browned crust on the protein.
steps.why: Browning builds deep flavour the stew layers on.
steps.watch_out: Don't crowd the pan — brown in batches.

steps.action: Heat the oil in a pot until very hot — a slice of onion should sizzle immediately.
steps.cue: Onion sizzles on contact.
steps.why: Hot oil cooks the raw tomato fast and clean.
steps.watch_out: Hot, not smoking.

steps.action: Add the sliced onion and fry 2 minutes, then pour in the blended mix SLOWLY (it splatters — step back).
steps.cue: The blend hits the oil and bubbles hard.
steps.why: Slow pouring controls the splatter.
steps.watch_out: Use a splatter screen or partial lid; hot stew burns.

steps.action: Fry the tomato mix on medium-high, stirring every 3 minutes, until thick and dark red with oil floating on top.
steps.cue: Mix is thick, deep brick-red, and oil pools at the surface.
steps.why: This long fry is the difference between bright, raw 'tomato sauce' and proper, mellow Nigerian stew. Don't rush it.
steps.watch_out: Lower the heat if it spits or catches; stir the bottom.

steps.action: Add the fried protein, stir, cover and cook 5 minutes. Taste for salt.
steps.cue: Protein is coated and the flavours meld.
steps.why: A short simmer marries the protein and stew.

doneness_signature: Thick, dark-red, oil-glossed stew with a deep cooked-down flavour — pairs with anything.

rescue.fix: It needs more frying time — keep cooking on medium until the rawness goes and the oil separates.
Skim oil from the top; it's traditional to leave some but you can remove excess.

level_up.how: Finish with a little ground ehu (calabash nutmeg) or a bay leaf while it simmers.

name: Boiled yam and egg sauce

difficulty.label: Easy
drivers: Two simple parts: boil yam, make a quick sauce
Hard to ruin — just don't overcook the yam

time.overlap_note: Make the egg sauce while the yam boils.

ingredients.prep: Peeled and cut into medium slices.

steps.action: Boil the yam slices in salted water until a fork goes in easily.
steps.cue: A fork slides in with no resistance, ~15-20 min.
steps.why: Yam should be tender but hold its shape.
steps.watch_out: Overcooking makes it fall apart and go gluey.

steps.action: While the yam boils, heat the oil and fry the onion until soft.
steps.cue: Onion soft and fragrant.
steps.why: Base for the sauce.

steps.action: Add the diced tomatoes and cook 3-4 minutes until softened.
steps.cue: Tomatoes break down into a loose sauce.
steps.why: Cooking off the raw tomato.

steps.action: Crack in the eggs. Stir immediately for soft scramble, or leave 2 minutes for a more set sauce. Season with salt (and crayfish).
steps.cue: Eggs just set, still glossy and soft.
steps.why: Eggs keep cooking off the heat — pull them slightly underdone.
steps.watch_out: Don't overcook to rubbery.

steps.action: Drain the yam and serve with the egg sauce over it.
steps.why: A pinch of crayfish in the sauce changes the whole flavour — try it.

doneness_signature: Tender white yam under a soft, glossy tomato-egg sauce.

rescue.fix: Mash it with a little oil and salt and serve as a quick yam mash instead.
Stir in a spoon of the tomato sauce off the heat to loosen them.

level_up.how: Add a blended scotch bonnet and a spoon of palm oil for a spicy, Niger-Delta-style egg sauce.

name: Ogbono soup

difficulty.label: Intermediate
drivers: Ogbono must be dissolved in oil correctly or it clumps and won't draw
Constant stirring needed to develop the draw
Timing the protein and the thickener together

time.overlap_note: Grind the ogbono while the protein cooks.

ingredients.prep: Ground dry to a fine powder (or buy pre-ground). Fresh-ground draws best.

steps.action: Cook the protein and stockfish with onion and stock cube until soft. Keep the stock.
steps.cue: Protein tender; flavourful stock.
steps.why: The stock is the soup's liquid base.
steps.watch_out: Don't let it dry out.

steps.action: In a separate small pot, warm the palm oil until liquid, take it OFF the heat, and stir in the ground ogbono.
steps.cue: It forms a smooth, glossy, nutty-smelling paste.
steps.why: Dissolving ogbono in warm (not boiling) oil off the heat is what lets it draw later. Added straight to water, it clumps into hard lumps.
steps.watch_out: Take the oil off the heat first — too hot and the ogbono fries instead of dissolving.

steps.action: Stir the ogbono-oil paste into the protein stock pot on medium heat.
steps.cue: The paste blends into the stock evenly.
steps.why: Now it disperses smoothly through the whole pot.
steps.watch_out: Stir as you add to avoid lumps re-forming.

steps.action: Add the crayfish and stir CONSTANTLY for about 5 minutes — ogbono thickens and draws as it cooks.
steps.cue: Lift the spoon and the soup pulls into strings.
steps.why: Constant stirring develops the draw evenly and stops it catching.
steps.watch_out: Stop stirring and it can clump or burn at the bottom.

steps.action: Taste for salt and add the shredded greens in the last 2 minutes if using.
steps.cue: Greens wilt, soup is thick and stretchy.
steps.why: Greens only need to wilt.

doneness_signature: Thick, dark, glossy soup that draws into long strings, rich with crayfish and palm oil.

rescue.fix: Lower the heat and mash the lumps against the pot side while stirring; they'll slowly dissolve.
Your ogbono may be old. Mix a little fresh ground ogbono with warm oil and stir it in.

level_up.how: Add assorted meats and dry fish for a heartier, special-occasion pot.

name: Nigerian spaghetti / one-pot pasta

difficulty.label: Easy
drivers: Straightforward: boil pasta, make sauce, combine
Hard to ruin — just don't overcook the pasta

time.overlap_note: Make the sauce while the pasta boils.

steps.action: Boil the pasta in salted water until cooked but not mushy. Drain and set aside.
steps.cue: Tender with a slight bite, ~8-10 min.
steps.why: It cooks a little more in the sauce, so stop just short.
steps.watch_out: Salt the water well — it's your one chance to season the pasta itself.

steps.action: In the same pot, heat the oil and fry the onion 2 minutes.
steps.cue: Onion soft.
steps.why: Base flavour.

steps.action: Add the blended tomatoes and fry 8 minutes until thick and oil shows on top.
steps.cue: Thick sauce, oil floating.
steps.why: Cooking out the raw tomato — same rule as stew.
steps.watch_out: Stir so it doesn't catch.

steps.action: Add the protein (raw: cook ~10 min with a splash of water; pre-cooked: add now), then curry, stock cube and salt.
steps.cue: Protein cooked, sauce seasoned.
steps.why: Build the sauce fully before the pasta goes in.

steps.action: Add the drained pasta and toss everything together on low heat for 2 minutes.
steps.cue: Every strand coated in sauce.
steps.why: Tossing in the pan flavours the pasta through, the Nigerian way — not served plain with sauce on top.
steps.watch_out: Low heat so the bottom doesn't catch.

doneness_signature: Tender, sauce-coated pasta, evenly red, with protein and a curry warmth.

rescue.fix: Toss with a tablespoon of oil and a splash of hot water to loosen.
Add a little hot water or extra sauce and toss.

level_up.how: Treat it like jollof — cook the drained pasta IN the sauce with a little stock for a smoky one-pot version.

name: Moi moi (steamed bean pudding)

difficulty.label: Involved
drivers: Peeling the beans by hand is slow, essential work
The batter consistency and seasoning must be judged before steaming
Long steam with a doneness test, and fillings to layer

time.overlap_note: Soak the beans ahead; the steam is hands-off once it's set up.

equipment: Moi moi moulds (tins, foil, or leaves)
Large pot with lid for steaming

ingredients.prep: Soaked 30 min, then rubbed between the palms to remove ALL the skins, rinsed clean.
substitutes: pre-peeled beans flour as a faster alternative

steps.action: After soaking, rub the beans between your palms to loosen the skins, then rinse the skins away in several changes of water until the beans are clean and white.
steps.cue: Beans are pale and skinless; the water runs clear of skins.
steps.why: Skins make moi moi grainy and grey. This is the effort-heavy step that makes the texture smooth — the old recipe hid it in the ingredient line.
steps.watch_out: Float the skins off the top — they rise while the heavy beans sink.

steps.action: Blend the peeled beans with the peppers and onion using minimal water to a thick, smooth batter.
steps.cue: Thick and smooth like cake batter — it should drop off the spoon in a ribbon, not pour.
steps.why: Too much water and the moi moi won't set. Thick batter is essential.
steps.watch_out: Add water a splash at a time; you can't take it back out.

steps.action: Stir in the oil, stock cube and salt. Taste the raw batter — it should be well seasoned.
steps.cue: Batter tastes pleasantly salty and savoury.
steps.why: You can't season it after steaming, so get it right now.
steps.watch_out: Under-seasoned batter = bland moi moi with no fix.

steps.action: Grease the moulds. Spoon batter halfway, add filling, top with more batter.
steps.cue: Moulds filled about 3/4 to leave room to rise.
steps.why: Layering puts the filling in the centre.
steps.watch_out: Don't overfill — it expands as it steams.

steps.action: Steam in a pot with water reaching halfway up the moulds, lid on, for 45-50 minutes. Top up water if it boils low.
steps.cue: A knife pushed into the centre comes out clean.
steps.why: Gentle steam sets the pudding evenly.
steps.watch_out: Don't let the pot boil dry. Keep the lid on to hold the steam.

steps.action: Rest 5 minutes before unmoulding.
steps.cue: Firm enough to hold its shape.
steps.why: It firms up as it cools slightly.

doneness_signature: Smooth, firm, savoury bean pudding that slices clean, speckled red from the pepper.

rescue.fix: Batter had too much water. Steam longer; next time blend thicker.
Beans weren't fully peeled. Nothing to do now, but peel more thoroughly next time.

level_up.how: Steam in banana leaves instead of tins for the traditional aroma and a beautiful presentation.
Layer boiled egg, flaked mackerel, and kpomo through the middle for a protein-rich centre.

name: Nigerian jambalaya (rice with everything)
surprise_note: Takes a standard GoLemon rice + protein + vegetable basket and turns it into a one-pot cajun-influenced dish most users wouldn't think to try from these ingredients.

difficulty.label: Intermediate
drivers: One-pot, but the browning-then-building sequence matters
Judging the rice-to-liquid ratio so it cooks without burning
Several components added in order

time.overlap_note: Blend and chop while the protein browns.

steps.action: Season the protein with salt, stock cube and paprika/suya spice. Brown it in oil in a wide pot on all sides — don't cook through. Set aside.
steps.cue: Golden-brown crust; still pink inside is fine.
steps.why: Browning is where the deep flavour comes from; it finishes cooking in the rice.
steps.watch_out: Don't crowd the pot or it steams instead of browning.

steps.action: In the same pot, fry the diced onion 2 minutes in the leftover oil.
steps.cue: Onion soft, picking up the browned bits.
steps.why: Those browned bits (fond) are pure flavour.

steps.action: Add the blended tomato-pepper and fry on high 10 minutes until thick.
steps.cue: Thick, darkened, oil showing.
steps.why: Cook out the raw tomato before the rice goes in.
steps.watch_out: Stir to stop it catching.

steps.action: Return the browned protein, add the carrot, then the washed rice. Stir to coat everything.
steps.cue: Rice glossy and coated in the red base.
steps.why: Coating the rice in the base flavours every grain.

steps.action: Add water to sit 1.5cm above the rice. Cover and cook on low 25-30 minutes. Check at 25.
steps.cue: Rice tender; protein cooked through; chunky and saucy.
steps.why: Low and covered lets it steam evenly without burning.
steps.watch_out: Undercooked at 25 min? Splash in a little water, cover, 5 more minutes.

doneness_signature: Smoky, saucy rice with visible chunky protein and flecks of carrot — heartier and chunkier than jollof.

rescue.fix: Sprinkle hot water over the top, cover, steam on lowest heat 8-10 min.
Don't stir up the burnt layer; move off heat, lid on, let steam finish it.

level_up.how: Add smoked sausage and a pinch of cayenne with the protein for a true jambalaya edge.

name: Plantain porridge (asaro-style)
surprise_note: Most users buy ripe plantain planning to fry it. This shows a savoury plantain porridge using the same ripe plantains — a completely different (and faster) dish.

difficulty.label: Simple
drivers: One-pot and forgiving
Only judgement is how soft and mashed you want the plantain

ingredients.prep: Peeled and cut into medium chunks.

steps.action: Heat the palm oil in a pot, add the onion and stir 1 minute.
steps.cue: Onion soft.
steps.why: Base flavour.
steps.watch_out: Don't smoke the palm oil.

steps.action: Add the blended tomato-pepper and fry 5 minutes.
steps.cue: Mix thickens and loses its raw smell.
steps.why: Cook out the rawness for a clean flavour.

steps.action: Add the plantain chunks and stir to coat in the base.
steps.cue: Plantain coated red.
steps.why: Coating flavours the plantain as it cooks.

steps.action: Add 1 cup water, cover, and cook on low 10-12 minutes until the plantain is soft.
steps.cue: A fork goes into the plantain easily.
steps.why: The plantain absorbs the tomato-oil flavour as it softens.
steps.watch_out: Don't add too much water — it should be a thick porridge, not a soup.

steps.action: Add crayfish, stock cube and salt. Mash some of the plantain to thicken, then stir in the torn scent leaf in the last minute.
steps.cue: Sweet, savoury, slightly smoky, thick.
steps.why: Mashing some chunks thickens the sauce; scent leaf finishes it.
steps.watch_out: Taste — plantain porridge balances sweet and savoury.

doneness_signature: Thick, sweet-savoury, smoky porridge of soft plantain in a red palm-oil sauce.

rescue.fix: Mash more plantain into it and simmer uncovered to thicken.
Add a little more pepper and salt to balance.

level_up.how: Add smoked fish or pre-cooked beef and a handful of ugu for a complete one-pot dinner.
